# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those seeking more control over their data and a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more data ownership and flexibility.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user per month.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to have full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, especially for large teams, since it can be self-hosted.
* Integration with Matrix protocol: Element has native support for the Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless communication with other Matrix-based platforms, while Slack does not.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and free
* Full control over data
* Highly customizable
* Native support for Matrix protocol
* Can be complex to set up and manage

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, and are willing to pay for these features. It is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that do not require a high level of customization or control over their data. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and flexibility, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server. It is suitable for large teams or organizations that require a high level of customization and control over their communication platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and create a new account.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure your Element server and set up any necessary integrations.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and manage. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's self-hosted setup can be complex and time-consuming, requiring a good understanding of server management and configuration. However, for teams that value data ownership and flexibility, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching to Element if you have a large team and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing your own server.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that require a high level of customization and control over their communication platform
* Teams that value data ownership and flexibility, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server
* Organizations that require a self-hosted solution for security or compliance reasons
* Teams that do not need a wide range of integrations, and are willing to use Element's native features instead
* Teams that are already familiar with the Matrix protocol and want to take advantage of its features

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means that you can use it without paying any subscription fees.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element can be more complex to set up and use than Slack, especially for non-technical users.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools and services?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations available, including support for the Matrix protocol.
### Is Element suitable for small teams?
Not necessarily, Element is more suitable for large teams or organizations that require a high level of customization and control over their communication platform.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

Both tools offer a core use case of real-time messaging, file sharing, and integrations, benefiting teams looking for a centralized collaboration space. The key reason someone would switch from Slack to Mattermost is to gain control over their data and reduce costs, especially for large teams or those with specific security requirements.

* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, especially for self-hosted instances, compared to Slack's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it suitable for large teams and organizations, while Slack also offers scalable plans but with limitations on free plans.
* Integration difference: Mattermost offers a more extensive API for custom integrations, whereas Slack has a wider range of pre-built integrations with popular tools.

|--------|----------|---------|

* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of pre-built integrations
* Scalable plans available
* Mobile apps for on-the-go access

### Mattermost
* Free, self-hosted option available
* High degree of customization and control
* Scalable and extensible architecture
* Integrates well with other open-source tools

# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Element is a free, self-hosted alternative to Discord. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control systems used for software development, offering a range of tools and features to manage code repositories, collaborate with team members, and track project progress. This comparison is beneficial for developers, project managers, and organizations looking to choose between the two platforms or considering switching from one to the other, particularly for reasons such as cost, data ownership, or specific feature requirements.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free and paid plans, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option.
* Data ownership: GitLab provides more control over data ownership due to its self-hosted option.
* Setup complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up, while GitLab requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: GitLab is more scalable due to its self-hosted option, which allows for greater control over infrastructure.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers built-in continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) features, while GitHub requires third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free and paid plans
* Limited control over data ownership
### GitLab
* Offers self-hosted option for greater control over data
* More scalable due to self-hosted option
* Built-in CI/CD features
* Free and open-source
* Can be complex to set up and manage

## When to Choose Each
### GitHub
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams or projects that require ease of use and integration with other GitHub tools. It is also suitable for teams that do not require a high level of control over their data or infrastructure. For example, a team of 10 developers working on a small web application may find GitHub's ease of use and integration with other tools to be beneficial.
### GitLab
GitLab is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their data and infrastructure. It is also suitable for teams that need built-in CI/CD features and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own instance. For example, a team of 50 developers working on a complex enterprise application may find GitLab's self-hosted option and built-in CI/CD features to be beneficial.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your repository's data.
2. Set up a new GitLab instance, either self-hosted or on GitLab.com.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to import your GitHub repository data into your new GitLab instance.
4. Update any existing links or integrations to point to your new GitLab instance.
5. Test your new GitLab instance to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
GitLab is production-ready for most users, offering a stable and feature-rich platform for software development. However, one technical limitation worth noting is that GitLab's self-hosted option can be complex to set up and manage, requiring significant technical expertise. Overall, we recommend switching to GitLab for teams that require a high level of control over their data and infrastructure, while smaller teams or projects may find GitHub's ease of use and integration with other tools to be more beneficial.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that require a high level of control over their data and infrastructure (less than 10 users)
* Medium-sized teams that need built-in CI/CD features (10-50 users)
* Large teams that require self-hosting for compliance or security reasons (more than 50 users)
* Teams that do not require integration with other GitHub tools
* Teams that are already familiar with GitLab or have existing infrastructure

## FAQ
### Can I use GitLab for free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free plan on GitLab.com.
### Is GitLab more secure than GitHub?
GitLab offers more control over data ownership and infrastructure, which can be beneficial for security-conscious teams.
### Can I integrate GitLab with other tools?
Yes, GitLab offers a range of integrations with other tools and services.
### Is GitLab suitable for small teams?
Yes, GitLab can be suitable for small teams, but may require more technical expertise to set up and manage.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, GitLab offers an import tool that allows you to migrate your GitHub repository data into your new GitLab instance.
